versions.label: EPRA 2024
versions.sub: S. 4753 (Manchin, Barrasso). Reported July 31, 2024. No floor vote.

versions.label: SPEED Act
versions.sub: H.R. 4776 (Westerman, Golden). Passed the House 221-196 on December 18, 2025.

current.text: States purposes only.

speed.text: Adds that NEPA is 'a purely procedural statute' that 'does not mandate particular results'.

senate.text: Adds that NEPA prescribes a procedure that ends in an informational document, and that nothing in it mandates a particular outcome.

current.text: Seven exclusions since 2023, including projects with minimal federal funding and loans where the agency lacks sufficient control.

speed.text: Adds grants and cost-share awards, Farm Service Agency loans, and actions another agency already reviewed. Federal money alone cannot make an action major.

senate.text: Fourteen exclusions. Adds loan-only projects, routine actions up to $10 million, lifeline infrastructure repair, geothermal test wells, in-corridor grid and gas pipeline work, previously reviewed actions, and Corps projects up to a $50 million federal share.

current.text: 'Reasonably foreseeable' effects. The Supreme Court held in 2025 that agencies need not study separate upstream or downstream projects.
current.cite: 42 U.S.C. 4332(2)(C); Seven County v. Eagle County

speed.text: Only effects proximately caused by the project itself. Speculative effects and effects of separate projects are excluded.

senate.text: No statutory limit on scope. Courts must give agencies substantial deference on the scope and contents of the document.

rows.topic: Ways to skip a full review

current.text: An agency's own categorical exclusions, or another agency's after consultation and public notice.

epra.text: Orders new categorical exclusions for renewable, geothermal and grid work on federal land.

speed.text: Adds exclusions enacted by Congress. Another statute or a state or tribal review can stand in for NEPA. A lead agency's finding that no document is needed binds other agencies.

senate.text: Same substitutes and the same binding rule, plus combining several exclusions on one project and a public CEQ register of every exclusion.

current.text: EIS in 2 years and EA in 1 year, counted from the earliest of the agency's determination, a complete application, or the notice of intent. Page limits of 150 and 75.

speed.text: Keeps the 2023 deadlines. Adds 60 days to judge an application complete and 60 days to pick the level of review.

senate.text: Same 2-year and 1-year deadlines and page limits, counted from the earlier of the agency's determination or a complete application. Same two 60-day front-end clocks.

current.text: No general deadline for the record of decision or for other agencies' permits.

epra.text: Project-specific clocks, such as 30 days to decide a renewable right-of-way once reviews are done.

speed.text: Final agency action within 30 days of the finished EIS or EA.

senate.text: Finding of no significant impact within 7 days of an EA. Record of decision within 45 days of an EIS. All federal permits within 90 days, or 120 days for agencies outside the review.

current.text: Agencies need not do new research unless it is essential and the cost and time are reasonable.

speed.text: No new research after an application arrives. No duty to consider research published after the earlier of the application or the notice of intent.

senate.text: No duty to consider research published after the notice of intent, and no delay to wait for it.

current.text: A reasonable range of alternatives that are feasible and meet the purpose and need.

speed.text: The statement of purpose and need must meet the applicant's goals.

senate.text: The lead agency must drop any alternative that misses the purpose and need or the non-federal sponsor's goals. The no-action alternative stays.

current.text: A sponsor may petition a court, which can order the agency to act within 90 days.

speed.text: Extensions only with the applicant's approval. A sponsor that approved one cannot petition a court unless the agency misses the new deadline.

senate.text: Once a deadline is 60 days overdue the agency head may not travel more than 25 miles from the duty station. Senior staff must spend half the workweek on the review when the agency has defied a CEQ dispute order. Courts must rule on a sponsor's petition within 120 days and can order a decision in 60.

current.text: Designates a lead agency within 40 days when agencies disagree. CEQ removed its own NEPA regulations in 2025 and 2026.

senate.text: The Chairman names lead agencies in 21 days and settles interagency disputes by final orders no court can review. CEQ runs a public permitting tracker, an ePermit portal targeted for December 1, 2028, and a $20 million-a-year improvement fund.

current.text: Reliable for 5 years without reevaluation.

speed.text: 10 years. Agencies may also reuse an earlier review of a substantially similar action.

senate.text: 10 years.

rows.topic: Time limit for a NEPA suit

current.text: 6 years by default, 2 years for FAST-41 projects, 150 days for highways and transit.

epra.text: 150 days for energy and mineral project decisions.

senate.text: 150 days.

current.text: Any party with standing that is adversely affected. No statutory comment requirement outside FAST-41.

speed.text: Only a party that filed a substantive and unique comment and suffers direct harm. No challenges to the creation of a categorical exclusion.

senate.text: Only a party alleging an actual or imminent injury amounting to direct harm. Where a comment period was offered, it must also have filed a detailed substantive comment.

current.text: District court, unless another statute sends the case to a court of appeals.

senate.text: The court of appeals for the circuit where the project sits, with randomly assigned judges.

current.text: Courts may vacate the approval or enjoin the project.

epra.text: Ordinary remedies. An agency gets no more than 180 days on remand.

speed.text: Remand only, without vacatur or injunction, with a fix due in 180 days. Applies to earlier court orders too.

senate.text: Remand only, without vacatur or injunction, with a fix due in 180 days. Work may continue during the remand. A preliminary injunction is possible when a different federal law is likely violated.

current.text: None.

speed.text: Judgment within 180 days of the agency record. Appeals decided in 180 days.

senate.text: Final judgment 'as expeditiously as possible'. No fixed deadline.

rows.topic: Suits over energy and mineral permits under any law

current.text: 6 years by default.

senate.text: 150 days. Remand capped at 180 days.

rows.topic: Suits under water, wildlife and historic preservation laws

current.text: 6 years, in district court, with ordinary remedies.

senate.text: 150 days for section 404 permits, biological opinions and section 106 decisions. Biological opinions go to the D.C. Circuit. Remand without vacatur for section 404 and section 106.

current.text: Allowed under each statute and permit, subject to ordinary court review.

speed.text: Barred except for a court order, breach, fraud, a specific and immediate harm, or the holder's request. Review in the court of appeals. The bill sets out no money damages.

senate.text: Barred, with the same five exceptions, for permits in effect on or after September 16, 2026. The agency carries the burden by clear and convincing evidence. A winning sponsor recovers fees, delay costs and 25 to 50 percent of project costs.

current.text: Agencies may ask a court to send their own approvals back.

speed.text: Exempt. The bill does not apply to any action an agency moved to reconsider after January 20, 2025.

senate.text: No exemption. Where a stop-work order from the year before enactment was enjoined, the same judge hears any new attempt.

current.text: No cause of action.

senate.text: Applicants in 46 named project types, plus any similar type a court certifies, can sue over an intentional pattern of delays or denials aimed at their project type. Damages run from 50 to 100 percent of expected construction cost.

rows.topic: Permits that need no environmental document

current.text: No general deadline.

epra.text: No general deadline. Clocks for particular permits only, such as wind, solar and geothermal applications.

senate.text: Decision within 1 year of a complete application for the listed project types, enforceable in court.

current.text: States certify compliance with water quality standards and other appropriate state law within a reasonable period of up to 1 year.

senate.text: Scope limited to water quality requirements. Denials and conditions need clear and convincing evidence. One-year cap, extendable only if the applicant and the state both agree in writing. Interstate pipelines and transmission lines get 9 months and are reviewed only for direct point-source discharges.

current.text: EPA may veto a fill site at any time. Nationwide permits and state discharge permits last 5 years. A 2020 court ruling required wildlife consultation to reissue a nationwide permit.

senate.text: EPA veto limited to the period between a complete application and the permit. Nationwide and discharge permits last 10 years. Nationwide permits that keep their preconstruction requirements are reissued without consultation, and fills under 2 acres count as minimal.

current.text: Formal consultation in 90 days, extendable. Only the federal wildlife agencies issue biological opinions.

epra.text: No change to consultation. Interior's approval of tribal right-of-way rules is exempt from the Act.

senate.text: 60 days, and no later than the NEPA deadline absent extraordinary circumstances. States may take over consultation under an agreement with Interior. $150 million a year authorized.

current.text: Agencies 'take into account' effects on historic properties under Advisory Council rules. No statutory deadlines. Visual and audible effects count.

epra.text: No change to the review. Interior's approval of tribal right-of-way rules is exempt from it.

senate.text: Statutory deadlines from start to finish. Adverse effects limited to direct alteration. Loans and grants alone do not trigger review. An agency may proceed when a preservation officer is silent for 30 days.

current.text: FERC can site a line only inside a corridor the Energy Department has designated, and only where a state lacks authority, has held an application for more than 1 year, or has set uneconomic conditions.

epra.text: FERC may permit lines of 100 kilovolts and up without a corridor.

senate.text: FERC shall permit lines of 230 kilovolts and up without a corridor. The state's clock starts on the day the application is filed with the state. Developers of lines of 345 kilovolts and up may file at FERC and the state together.

current.text: Regional planning required by FERC Orders 1000 and 1920. Interregional work is coordination only.

epra.text: Joint interregional plans required within 2 years. FERC resolves disputes and can impose a plan.

senate.text: Regional and interregional planning processes required within 2 years. Order No. 1920 compliance counts for the regional part. FERC can extend a late filing by 6 months.

current.text: Beneficiaries pay, roughly in proportion to benefits, under FERC and court precedent.

epra.text: Beneficiaries pay under the cost-causation principle. No involuntary charges for trivial benefits.

senate.text: Same rule, with costs 'at least roughly commensurate' with six listed benefits.

current.text: Covered by agency categorical exclusions in some cases.

epra.text: Interior and Agriculture adopt categorical exclusions within 180 days.

senate.text: Reconductoring, voltage increases and added circuits in existing rights-of-way are outside NEPA and section 106 by statute. So are gas pipeline looping and compression in existing corridors.

rows.topic: Data centers and other large loads

current.text: No federal floor. Retail costs are set in state rate cases and utility tariffs. FERC's 1994 transmission pricing policy lets a utility charge a new transmission customer the higher of embedded cost or incremental expansion cost, not the sum of the two. It may price separate lines on different bases.

senate.text: New Federal Power Act section 228 covers data center and high-density computing loads of 20 megawatts or more, counting phased buildouts and commonly controlled sites. Those that connect after enactment pay the full incremental cost of serving them, even after they leave; arrangements approved earlier stay in effect. States may auction access, require new generation, and require curtailable service. Separately, and with no size threshold, FERC must charge computing loads both the embedded and the incremental cost of transmission service. The Energy Information Administration must collect data center load.

note.label: Earlier bill
note.text: The Ratepayer Protection Act (H.R. 9340) would ask state regulators to consider making data centers of 100 megawatts or more pay the full incremental cost of upgrades, including after they leave, with financial assurance before construction. States would not have to adopt it. It passed the House 417-3 on September 16, 2026, and the Senate rejected cloture 57-43 on September 30. BAAJA section 228 uses similar terms but makes them binding at 20 megawatts, and section 2107(a) adds an embedded-cost charge for transmission. Harvard's Ari Peskoe called the House bill's consider standard 'largely symbolic', since Congress cannot force state regulators to act, and called BAAJA's data center rules 'an improvement on the status quo'.

sources.cite: H.R. 9340, as passed by the House
CBS News on the 417-3 House vote
Heatmap on the Ratepayer Protection Act
Heatmap on the Senate bill's data center rules

current.text: Cluster studies under FERC Order No. 2023.

senate.text: Interconnection planned with transmission over 20 years, with published per-megawatt prices and nonrefundable deposits. Automation required in queue studies. Grid data due in 15 days.

current.text: Planners must consider them under Order No. 1920.

epra.text: Advanced conductors eligible for backstop permits.

senate.text: Utilities must deploy them when benefits exceed costs, or face a lower return on equity.

current.text: FERC removed the federal right in 2011 and allowed it again for some replacement lines in Order No. 1920.

senate.text: Banned for regionally or interregionally planned lines.

current.text: Little federal review of projects a utility plans for itself.

senate.text: States can refer a utility to FERC. Remedies include a lower return and fines up to $5 million per facility.

current.text: Wholesale market access by rule under FERC Order No. 2222.

senate.text: Statutory wholesale market access for aggregations of 100 kilowatts and up, with a ban on double payment.

groups.label: Energy on federal land and water

current.text: A federal drilling permit is required whenever a well taps federal minerals. Five routine activities get a rebuttable categorical exclusion.

epra.text: No federal permit where the federal mineral share is under 50 percent on non-federal land. Lease nominations offered as submitted. Drilling permits last 4 years.

senate.text: No federal permit where the federal mineral share is under 50 percent on non-federal land. The five routine activities are outside NEPA entirely.

current.text: Leasing at Interior's discretion, with no decision deadlines.

epra.text: Deadlines for coal lease reviews and decisions.

senate.text: No leasing provisions. Coal appears only in the list of project types protected from unequal treatment.

rows.topic: Wind, solar and storage on public land

current.text: No application deadlines. A 2020 goal of 25 gigawatts by 2025.

epra.text: 30-day clocks, small-project exclusions, and a goal of 50 gigawatts by 2030.

senate.text: The same 30-day clocks and small-project exclusions. No gigawatt goal.

current.text: Offshore wind leasing is tied to oil and gas lease sales by the Inflation Reduction Act.

epra.text: One oil and gas sale and one wind sale every year through 2029, 400,000 acres of wind a year, and a 30-gigawatt wind goal.

senate.text: No lease sale mandates. Changes Interior's offshore wind test to 'unreasonable interference' with other uses and orders planned offshore transmission routes.

current.text: Energy Department public-interest review with no deadline.

epra.text: Decision within 90 days of the environmental review, or the application is deemed granted.

senate.text: No export provisions. LNG projects appear in the list of project types protected from unequal treatment.

current.text: Lease sales at least every 2 years.

epra.text: Annual lease sales, 30-day permit decisions, an ombudsman, and exclusions for test wells.

senate.text: All of that, plus a per-plant royalty clock, no federal permit on minority-interest land, processing during lawsuits, and a NEPA exemption for routine drilling.

current.text: Federal land agencies set mandatory license conditions.

epra.text: License extensions, a market barriers report, and aligned timetables.

senate.text: The market barriers report, a limit on mandatory conditions, no approval for routine maintenance, and a 1-year deadline for FERC to decide small hydrokinetic licenses.

current.text: Mill sites are capped at 5 acres each. A 2022 appeals court ruling barred waste storage on claims without valuable minerals.

epra.text: As many mill sites as reasonably necessary, with fees paid into a cleanup fund.

senate.text: Same as EPRA 2024.

current.text: Interior must approve rights-of-way across tribal land.

epra.text: Tribes may grant their own rights-of-way under approved tribal rules.

speed.text: No NEPA suits over tribal trust resource projects except by the tribe. The no-action alternative is presumed harmful for tribe-initiated projects.

senate.text: Both: tribal rights-of-way, the limit on NEPA suits, and the no-action presumption.

added.text: Money damages when an agency unlawfully pulls a permit, and a cause of action for unequal treatment of 46 named project types.
Cost rules for data centers of 20 megawatts and up, and federal data on their electricity use.
Clean Water Act changes: state certification, EPA's veto, permit terms, nationwide permits.
Endangered Species Act changes: shorter consultation, state assumption, a definition of best available data.
A rewrite of historic preservation review under section 106.
CEQ dispute orders, sanctions for missed deadlines, a public tracker and the ePermit portal.
NEPA exemptions for gas pipeline work in existing corridors and for routine oil, gas and geothermal drilling.
Grid rules: local transmission oversight, the right-of-first-refusal ban, joint interconnection planning, mandatory advanced technologies, grid data access.
Wholesale market access for aggregated customer-sited storage and generation.

dropped.text: The limit on effects an agency may study to those proximately caused by the project.
The exemption for approvals an agency moved to reconsider after January 20, 2025.
The bar on suits challenging the creation of a categorical exclusion.
Fixed 180-day deadlines for court judgments and appeals.
Applying the remand-only rule to court orders issued before enactment.
The ban on withdrawing a finished environmental document, and on seeking a voluntary remand without the sponsor's consent.
Annual offshore oil and gas and offshore wind lease sales through 2029, and the 30-gigawatt offshore wind goal.
The 90-day deadline for LNG export decisions.
The goal of 50 gigawatts of renewable energy on federal land by 2030.
Onshore oil and gas lease nomination changes and 4-year drilling permits.
Reliability assessments of other agencies' proposed rules.
FERC's power to settle disputes between planning regions and impose an interregional plan.
Hydropower license extensions and aligned licensing timetables.

bills.label: Data center bills
bills.intro: BAAJA's data center and load-growth rules beside the federal bills that would regulate large computing loads, transmission pricing, and interconnection speed. EPRA 2024 and the SPEED Act did not address data center ratepayer rules or non-firm transmission service. Each cell links to the text it summarizes.

versions.label: Current policy
versions.sub: The White House Ratepayer Protection Pledge (March 2026) and FERC's June 18, 2026 show cause orders. FERC set no large-load rule.

versions.label: Ratepayer Protection Act (H.R. 9340)
versions.sub: Evans (R-Colo.) and Castor (D-Fla.). House-passed text, September 16, 2026. Senate cloture failed September 30; vote sources are in the large-load comparison note.

versions.label: GRID Savings Act (S. 5199)
versions.sub: Heinrich (D-N.M.), August 2026. In committee; a unanimous-consent request failed September 17.

versions.label: Power for the People Act (S. 3682)
versions.sub: Van Hollen (D-Md.), January 2026; House companion H.R. 8241 (Tonko). In committee.

versions.label: GRID Act (S. 3852)
versions.sub: Hawley (R-Mo.) and Blumenthal (D-Conn.), February 11, 2026. In committee.

policy.text: The Pledge: seven hyperscalers and AI companies, later joined by governors, developers and power providers. FERC's June 2026 orders: the six regional grid operators.
policy.quote: President Trump is calling on the leading United States hyperscalers and AI companies to build, bring, or buy all of the energy needed for building and operating data centers

rpa.text: Data centers with 100 MW or more of peak demand at one site or campus, contracting after enactment. The introduced bill covered any 100 MW load; committee narrowed it.
rpa.quote: require electric energy primarily to operate information technology infrastructure and related systems pertaining to data storage and computational applications and services

grid_savings.text: Any new or expanded non-residential load of 150 MW or more at one interconnection, counting affiliated sites and phases. Not limited to data centers.
grid_savings.quote: has an aggregate requested or projected peak electric demand of not less than 150 megawatts behind a single point of interconnection

pftp.text: Data centers drawing more than 50 MW, counting same-owner facilities in one utility area. Crypto mines are defined separately.
pftp.quote: has an energy demand greater than 50 megawatts

grid_act.text: Private data centers of 20 MW or more, existing or planned within 5 years. Federal data centers excluded.
grid_act.quote: with a power demand of 20 megawatts or more that is not owned, operated, or maintained

senate.text: Section 228: data centers and high-density computing, including crypto mining, of 20 MW or more at one site or at commonly controlled sites, counting phased buildouts. Section 2107(a) pricing: any computational load on the bulk-power system, no size threshold. Ancillary computing at other commercial or industrial facilities is excluded from section 228.

policy.text: Mostly voluntary. The Pledge creates no legal duty. FERC's June 18 orders find grid operators' tariffs may be unjust and make them justify or rewrite them. No final FERC rule.
policy.quote: The Ratepayer Protection Pledge and the commitments embodied therein effectuate the national policy of the United States.

rpa.text: Optional. A PURPA standard each state must consider within 1 year and decide within 2. States need not adopt it.
rpa.quote: shall commence consideration under section 111, or set a hearing date for consideration

grid_savings.text: Binding. New Federal Power Act section 224 gives FERC jurisdiction over large-load interconnection; final rule within 1 year.
grid_savings.quote: the Commission shall issue a final rule, applicable to each transmitting utility, establishing standards and procedures for the interconnection of covered large loads

pftp.text: Mixed. FERC must order transmission cost tariffs (120 days) and a data center queue rule (180 days). The rate class is a PURPA standard states must consider.
pftp.quote: the Commission shall issue a rule requiring all covered interconnection entities to create, for the purpose of addressing reliability and affordability concerns from new data center loads

grid_act.text: Binding prohibition enforced by DOE, with penalties of at least $1 million a day.
grid_act.quote: a covered entity may not build, own, operate, or maintain a data center unless the data center derives all of its energy

senate.text: Binding. Section 228 is a federal floor in the Federal Power Act. Section 2107(a) orders FERC to revise its 1994 pricing policy in 270 days, propose a rule 270 days later and finish within a year.

policy.text: Pledge signers say they will pay for the new generation and grid upgrades their data centers need. Retail costs otherwise follow state rate cases.
policy.quote: Companies will pay for all new power delivery infrastructure upgrades required to service their data centers

rpa.text: Rates recover from the data center the full incremental cost of generation, transmission or distribution upgrades needed to serve it.
rpa.quote: shall be designed to recover from the large-load customer the full, incremental cost of any generation, transmission, or distribution upgrade necessary to serve the load of such large-load customer

grid_savings.text: The load pays all interconnection and direct-assignment costs. Network upgrades are charged to it and credited back against its transmission bills, as for generators. Generation and distribution are not covered.
grid_savings.quote: directly assigned to, and fully borne by, the applicable covered large-load customer

pftp.text: Data centers pay local transmission upgrades that exist only because of them. States must consider a rate class that recovers the full cost of upgrades.
pftp.quote: allocate to each interconnecting data center local transmission upgrade costs that, but for the existence of the data center, would not be needed

grid_act.text: No cost allocation rule. New data centers must be off the grid; existing ones must show they do not raise rates or pay credits.
grid_act.quote: will not increase the electrical rates paid by ratepayers

senate.text: No incremental cost of serving a covered load (generation, storage, transmission, distribution) may be recovered from other customers.

policy.text: FERC's 1994 transmission pricing policy allows the higher of embedded cost or incremental expansion cost for a service, rather than their sum. Separate lines may be priced on different bases.

rpa.text: Transmission upgrades fall under the state standard. No FERC role and no embedded-cost charge.
rpa.quote: any generation, transmission, or distribution upgrade necessary to serve the load of such large-load customer

grid_savings.text: FERC classifies and allocates facilities under interconnection rules adapted for loads. A load may fund regional lines in exchange for transmission rights.
grid_savings.quote: to voluntarily fund all or a portion of a transmission facility selected in a regional or interregional transmission plan

pftp.text: Two parts: direct assignment of local upgrades, plus rates reflecting the embedded cost of the grid.
pftp.quote: require data centers to pay transmission rates applicable to their rate class that reflect the embedded cost of the integrated grid

grid_act.text: No transmission pricing rule and no FERC role.
grid_act.quote: how interconnection costs and other infrastructure costs needed to supply the data center with power from the electric grid are allocated

senate.text: Computational loads pay both the embedded and the incremental cost of transmission. Incremental payments are credited to the utility's revenue requirement so other customers are not charged twice.

policy.text: Pledge signers say they will pay negotiated rates whether or not they use the power.
policy.quote: Importantly, they will pay these rates for the power and related infrastructure that are brought online to service their data centers, whether they use the electricity or not

rpa.text: Recovery continues if the customer ends its contract or stops buying power.
rpa.quote: including in the event of such large-load customer terminating a contract or other agreement with the electric utility

grid_savings.text: Financial security must protect other customers if the load fails to proceed or perform.
grid_savings.quote: financial security designed to protect any customer from unrecovered costs if a covered large load fails to proceed or perform

pftp.text: States must consider longer minimum contracts and minimum demand charges.
pftp.quote: an extension of minimum utility contract lengths for data center customers to ensure that data center load does not leave utilities and ratepayers with stranded costs

senate.text: Recovery continues if the data center ends its contract or stops buying power before the incremental cost is paid off.

policy.text: FERC's June orders call for rising readiness requirements to deter speculative requests.
policy.cite: Utility Dive on FERC's June 2026 orders
policy.quote: We target speculative projects by establishing escalating readiness requirements for distinct phases of the study process to deter duplicative or speculative requests for transmission service,

rpa.text: The utility must require assurances or contributions before building an upgrade.
rpa.quote: an electric utility shall require the large-load customer provide to the electric utility financial assurances or contributions to cover the cost of such upgrade

grid_savings.text: FERC's rule sets payment and security requirements.
grid_savings.quote: financial security designed to protect any customer from unrecovered costs if a covered large load fails to proceed or perform

pftp.text: States must consider higher study fees, deposits or collateral, and up-front construction contributions.
pftp.quote: an increase in up-front interconnection study costs, deposit amounts, or collateral requirements for data center projects

senate.text: Before building or upgrading generation, transmission or distribution for the load, the utility must collect assurances or contributions covering the cost.

policy.text: Pledge signers say they will negotiate separate rate structures with utilities and states.
policy.quote: Companies will voluntarily negotiate new, separate rate structures with their utilities and relevant State governments wherever they build data centers.

pftp.text: States must consider a data center rate class. DOE grants help them.
pftp.quote: establishing a rate class specific to data centers to ensure that data center owners and operators are covering the full cost of the generation, transmission, and distribution upgrades necessary to serve data centers

grid_act.text: DOE must put residential customers' rates ahead of every other class.
grid_act.quote: the Secretary shall prioritize the electrical rates paid by residential ratepayers over all other ratepayer classes

senate.text: States may make data centers a separate class with rates, terms and interconnection priorities less favorable than other large industrial loads.

policy.text: FERC wants standard large-load applications and studies in each region.
policy.quote: Develop standardized transmission service applications and study processes for large loads

grid_savings.text: Study timelines and readiness requirements against speculative requests. No open seasons.
grid_savings.quote: protect other customers from the costs of speculative or duplicative requests

pftp.text: Grid operators run a data center queue that favors those offsetting their demand, and may delay or deny connections that hurt reliability or affordability.
pftp.quote: a data center that is not already interconnected with the electric grid may not interconnect with the electric grid unless the data center has fully advanced through the applicable data center load queue system

senate.text: States may run open seasons that award service by greatest benefit to other ratepayers, whatever the order of requests.

policy.text: Pledge signers say they will build, bring or buy new generation. FERC told grid operators to address co-location.
policy.quote: Companies will build, bring, or buy the new generation resources and electricity needed to satisfy their new energy demands

grid_savings.text: Optional. A load may be studied with its own generation, storage or flexibility.
grid_savings.quote: the study and interconnection, separately or together, of a covered large load and any associated generation, energy storage, or verifiable load flexibility

pftp.text: Queue priority for data centers that bring new low- or no-carbon supply they pay for. Not required.
pftp.quote: are designated for the service of, and paid for by, the data center owner or operator, including through a power purchase agreement or another bilateral contract

grid_act.text: Starting 180 days after enactment, new data centers must take all power, including backup, from sources separate from the grid. Existing grid-connected centers have a 10-year transition under DOE certificates.
grid_act.quote: derives all of its energy, including back-up energy, from a captive power plant, on-site power generation, or some other source or combination of sources separate from, and not deriving power from, the electric grid

senate.text: States may require the data center to procure, build or contract for new generation sufficient to serve it.

policy.text: FERC asked grid operators for new transmission services for flexible large loads.
policy.cite: Utility Dive on FERC's June 2026 orders
policy.quote: new transmission services for flexible large loads

grid_savings.text: Flexible and phased interconnection service at the customer's election.
grid_savings.quote: flexible interconnection service, subject to enforceable operating limits

pftp.text: Flexibility agreements let the operator curtail data centers before other users and can count toward the supply they must bring.
pftp.quote: data centers may be interrupted by the covered interconnection entity

senate.text: States may require service that limits how much or when the load draws power. FERC must price non-firm transmission service lower.

grid_savings.text: Upgrade payments are credited back to the paying load, not to other customers.
grid_savings.quote: those costs shall be credited back against transmission service charges

grid_act.text: Grid-connected data centers can pay Rate Effect Credits to offset their effect on rates.
grid_act.quote: a credit paid by a covered entity to an appropriate party, as determined by the Secretary, that offsets the effect that a data center would otherwise have on the electrical rates paid by ratepayers

senate.text: States may charge more than cost and credit the surplus to other customers.

policy.text: The Pledge covers new demand only.

rpa.text: Applies to customers that request service or contract after enactment. States that already acted on a comparable standard are exempt.
rpa.quote: on or after the date of the enactment of this paragraph, requests to enter into, or enters into, a contract or other agreement

grid_savings.quote: a new or expanded nonresidential electric load

pftp.text: The queue covers data centers not yet connected. The text does not say how the tariff or rate class treats existing sites.
pftp.quote: a data center that is not already interconnected with the electric grid may not interconnect

grid_act.text: Existing data centers get 10 years to leave the grid, operating meanwhile under one-year DOE certificates.
grid_act.quote: Until the date that is 10 years after the date of enactment of this Act, a covered entity that owns, operates, or maintains an existing data center that derives any of its energy from the electric grid

senate.text: Section 228(b) cost protection and (c) state open-season authority apply to covered loads interconnecting on or after enactment. Previously approved service arrangements remain in effect. Section 2107(a) transmission pricing has no express existing-load exemption; its scope is separate.

policy.text: FERC found grid operators' upgrade costs are not transparent. No EIA change.
policy.cite: Utility Dive on FERC's June 2026 orders
policy.quote: lack of transparency in how RTOs and ISOs determine how network upgrades are assigned and paid for

grid_savings.text: Each load, state commission and FERC get the classification, costs and alternatives studied.

pftp.text: FERC sets disclosure rules for interconnection requests. DOE helps with load forecasts.
pftp.quote: the Commission shall establish transparency and disclosure requirements for data center load interconnection requests

grid_act.text: DOE sets public disclosure of usage, property deals and utility agreements.
grid_act.quote: the Secretary shall establish a national requirement for covered entities to provide to the public

senate.text: EIA must add data center load to Form 861, with no 20 MW threshold in section 2114. Revision is due at least 90 days before the first April 1 after enactment.

policy.text: FERC's 1994 pricing policy allows discounted or negotiated rates, but sets no mandatory transmission rate discount for flexible or non-firm computing loads.

grid_savings.text: Directs FERC to provide flexible interconnection service, but establishes no statutory rate discount for non-firm service.

pftp.text: Allows curtailable service agreements to satisfy clean energy requirements, but specifies no discounted transmission rate.

senate.text: FERC must revise its transmission pricing policy within 270 days to provide a lower transmission price for computational loads electing non-firm service. Studies must evaluate standardized cost-reduction options to avoid network upgrades.

policy.text: Order 2023 set cluster studies and study deadlines; FERC's June 2026 show cause orders asked grid operators for large-load study timelines, but set no automation requirements.

grid_savings.text: Sets study schedules and readiness requirements to curb speculative requests, but mandates no AI or automation in study software.

pftp.text: Creates a dedicated data center queue; grid operators may delay or deny studies for loads that threaten reliability.

senate.text: Directs FERC within 1 year to require AI and automation in interconnection study evaluations. Mandates 15-day grid data turnaround under reliability penalties, and requires a joint FERC/DOE reference spec for fully automated studies within 1 year.

policy.text: FERC Order No. 1920 requires transmission planners to evaluate dynamic line ratings, advanced power flow control, and advanced conductors, but deployment is voluntary.

senate.text: Utilities must deploy advanced transmission technologies whenever benefits exceed costs, backed by ROE reduction penalties. In-corridor reconductoring and grid capacity expansions are categorically excluded from NEPA and NHPA reviews.

policy.text: FERC Order No. 2222 required grid operators to allow distributed energy resource aggregations into wholesale markets, but implementation is delayed across several regions.

senate.text: Bars grid operators from blocking qualifying behind-the-meter aggregations from wholesale markets. Distribution utilities in organized markets must interconnect them; device-level inverter telemetry allowed.

others.text: Data Center Transparency Act (H.R. 6984; Menendez, Casar): EIA would collect each data center's energy use every six months; EPA would report on water use and emissions. No cost rules.

Protecting Ratepayers Act (H.R. 9777; Donalds): data centers of 5 MW or more, existing ones included, would have to take all power and water from sources separate from the public grid and water system within 180 days, and the Pledge proclamation would gain the force of law.

Clean Cloud Act (S. 1475; Whitehouse, Fetterman): an EPA emissions standard and fee for data centers and crypto mines over 100 kW, with annual EIA reporting. A utility may not pass the fee to other customers.
